summary: This standards-track document defines a voucher, an artifact signed directly or indirectly by a device's manufacturer, used to securely assign the device (the pledge) to an owner. The voucher is a YANG-defined JSON document signed with the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is part of bootstrapping protocols for new devices.

plainLanguage.summary: A new gadget needs proof of who owns it. The maker signs a note that says 'this belongs to you,' like a paper receipt.

questions: how does a new device securely find its owner
what is a masa in bootstrapping
what is a pledge in device onboarding
what is the pinned domain cert
subtitle: A signed note from a device's maker that tells a brand-new device which network owner to trust.

tldr.problem: A new device (the pledge) ships trusting only its manufacturer, so it needs a safe way to learn which domain is its rightful owner and to avoid being taken over by a man-in-the-middle registrar.
tldr.mechanism: The manufacturer's signing service (the MASA) issues a voucher: a YANG-defined JSON document, CMS-signed by default, that carries the pledge's serial number and a pinned-domain-cert the pledge can use to authenticate the owner's domain.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8366 defines only the voucher artifact, not the protocols that fetch it. It recommends short-lived, renewable vouchers rather than revocation.

today: RFC 8366 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It defines only the voucher artifact; the protocols that obtain vouchers are left to other documents, which the RFC names as BRSKI, a 6tisch secure join protocol and NETCONF zero-touch.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8366 defines a strategy to securely assign a candidate device, called a pledge, to an owner. The assignment is an artifact signed, directly or indirectly, by the pledge's manufacturer. That artifact is the voucher.

The voucher is a JSON document that follows a YANG data model and is signed using, by default, a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) structure. Its main job is to convey one certificate, the pinned-domain-cert, which the pledge uses to authenticate later interactions. The driving motivation is secure bootstrapping: the pledge needs to authenticate the network that is trying to take control of it.

The document only defines the voucher itself. It leaves the protocols for accessing it to other documents and names bootstrapping protocols such as BRSKI as users of it.
sections.plainLanguage: When you plug in a new gadget, it needs to know whose it is. The voucher is a signed note from the company that made it, naming the owner the gadget should trust.

sections.title: The Cast of Characters
sections.content:
The RFC uses a small vocabulary.

  • Pledge: the prospective device trying to find and securely join a domain. When shipped, it only trusts authorized representatives of the manufacturer.
  • MASA (Manufacturer Authorized Signing Authority): the entity that signs vouchers for a manufacturer's pledges. In some protocols it is an online service, in others an offline one.
  • Join registrar (or just registrar): a representative of the domain that decides whether a new device may join.
  • Domain: the set of entities or infrastructure under common administrative control.
  • Owner: whoever controls the private key of the certificate named in the voucher.
  • Imprint: the process where a device obtains the key material it needs to trust future interactions with a network.
  • TOFU (Trust on First Use): the pledge simply trusts the first domain entity that contacts it.

The word imprint comes from ducklings that treat the first thing that looks like a mother as their mother. A device that imprints on an attacker suffers a similar fate to a duckling that imprints on a hungry wolf.
sections.plainLanguage: A new gadget is like a baby duckling that follows the first thing it sees. The voucher makes sure the gadget follows its real owner and not a wolf in disguise.

sections.title: Voucher Types
sections.content:
A voucher can tell the pledge and registrar three kinds of things: an assertion basis (how the imprint is protected, for example logging or verified ownership), how the pledge can authenticate the join registrar (this document defines pinning the domain certificate), and anti-replay protection (time or nonce based).

Different mixes of these give named voucher types, all aimed at the main threat of a man-in-the-middle registrar taking over the pledge:

  • Audit Voucher: the registrar audits logs to confirm no unknown registrar appears. The MASA does not need to know actual ownership.
  • Nonceless Audit Voucher: an Audit Voucher with no validity period statement, so it can be issued in advance, for example for network partitions or remote deployments.
  • Ownership Audit Voucher: the MASA has verified the registrar as the authorized owner and refuses to issue vouchers for unauthorized registrars.
  • Ownership ID Voucher: names the registrar's CN-ID or DNS-ID, so the MASA identifies the specific registrar authorized to own the pledge.
  • Bearer Voucher: uses a wildcard registrar ID, so anyone holding it can claim the pledge. Bearer vouchers are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some notes say 'this gadget goes to Sam', some say 'check the logbook first', and a risky kind says 'whoever holds this note can have the gadget'. The RFC leaves out that last kind.

sections.title: The Voucher Data Model
sections.content:
The voucher is one voucher container defined in a YANG module named ietf-voucher. Its leaves are:

  • created-on (required): when the voucher was created, mainly for humans and auditing.
  • expires-on (optional): when it expires. If present, the pledge MUST ensure the time has not passed, so a pledge without an accurate clock cannot meet this. It cannot be combined with nonce.
  • assertion (required): one of verified, logged or proximity. Pledges MUST check that the assertion is acceptable under local policy.
  • serial-number (required): the pledge MUST confirm it matches its own, or it MUST NOT process the voucher.
  • idevid-issuer (optional): the Authority Key Identifier from the pledge's IDevID certificate, for serial numbers that are not otherwise unique within the MASA.
  • pinned-domain-cert (required): an X.509 v3 certificate in DER encoding. The domain certificate supplied separately by the bootstrapping protocol MUST have it somewhere in its chain.
  • domain-cert-revocation-checks (optional): tells the pledge it MUST (true) or MUST NOT (false) check revocation status of the pinned certificate.
  • nonce (optional, 8 to 32 bytes): must match a random value the pledge sent earlier, for anti-replay.
  • last-renewal-date (optional, informative): the last date the MASA expects to renew the voucher.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has blanks to fill in: when it was written, which gadget it is for (by serial number), and which owner's ID card the gadget should trust. The gadget checks every blank before it believes the note.

sections.title: Signing and Encoding the Voucher
sections.content:
By default the voucher is CMS-signed. A CMS SignedData structure, DER encoded, wraps the JSON, and an eContentType of 40 marks the content as a JSON-encoded voucher. The RFC registers the media type application/voucher-cms+json and the filename extension .vcj.

The CMS structure MUST contain a signerInfo with a signature made by a private key the recipient trusts. Normally the recipient is the pledge and the signer is the MASA. It SHOULD also include the certificates up to and including the signer's trust anchor, because third parties cannot audit the transaction without it. CRLs and similar mechanisms are discouraged, since a pledge is unlikely to be able to perform online checks or to have a trusted clock.

The document expects future work to map the voucher to CBOR and to use JOSE or COSE instead of CMS.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is sealed with the maker's special stamp. The gadget knows the stamp, so it can tell the note is real and has not been changed.

sections.title: Design Choices: Renewals and One Voucher Per Pledge
sections.content:
Revocation lists add extra protocols and code paths, and a pledge might skip the check if, for example, an OCSP responder is unreachable. The RFC instead recommends lightweight renewals of short-lived, non-revocable vouchers. The MASA sets expires-on to a near date and promises, through last-renewal-date, to reissue when needed. The first issue may need heavy checks of who is asking and whether the pledge belongs to them, but a renewal only updates the validity period.

A voucher may still be effectively revoked if one of the intermediate CA certificates that signed it is revoked. The format does not forbid long-lived vouchers, but no revocation method is described for them.

Early versions let one voucher cover many pledges using regular expressions over serial numbers. That was dropped because blocking renewal for one device would block all of them, so a voucher now lists a single serial number.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a note that lasts forever and needs a 'cancelled' list, the maker gives short notes and quickly writes a new one when asked. If the maker stops writing new ones, the old one simply runs out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clock sensitivity is the first concern. An attacker could replay an expired voucher to a device with no sense of time, and the device cannot trust NTP because an attacker could control it. Defences are: devices must check expires-on, devices without time can use nonces to get ephemeral vouchers, and vouchers without expiry show up in the audit log. Vendors issuing vouchers with expirations must ensure devices ship with an accurate clock and prevent tampering, otherwise they should not issue expiring vouchers.

The MASA's signing key is RECOMMENDED to be protected by a hardware security module. If a domain certificate is compromised, the domain administrator is expected to revoke it and to ask the MASA to block automated renewal of outstanding vouchers.

CMS signing protects the voucher from modification but not from being read. Observers could learn which devices belong to which organizations. When privacy matters, the signed data SHOULD be encrypted, either by carrying it over a mutually authenticated secure transport such as TLS or by wrapping it in an enveloped-data content type.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal stops anyone changing the note, but anyone can still read it. If the note is private, put it in a locked box when you send it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered four things: the XML namespace URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-voucher in the IETF XML Registry, the YANG module ietf-voucher with prefix vch, the media type application/voucher-cms+json with file extension .vcj, and CMS content type OID 40, id-ct-animaJSONVoucher, in the SMI Security for S/MIME CMS Content Type registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks the internet's librarian to write down the names it invented so nobody else uses them for something different.

items.label: Verified
items.desc: Ownership positively verified by the MASA, for example through sales channel integration.

items.label: Logged
items.desc: Issued after minimal verification, with issuance logged so unexpected vouchers can be detected.

items.label: Proximity
items.desc: Issued after the MASA verified a proximity proof from the device and target domain; also logged.
